summary: A proposal from MITRE and UCLA authors for helping new ARPANET users who were not tied to any server site. It supports the NIC's suggestion of a working group on user information and services and offers a specific idea for that group's meeting. The Resources Notebook was then the main source of network-wide information.

eli5.summary: As more people started using the network, two authors suggested a team to help newcomers find out what is available and how to use it.

questions: how to find services on the arpanet
subtitle: Organizing help for new ARPANET users through a distributed information database.

tldr.problem: The growing ARPANET had more users, but they struggled to find information about available services. Centralized compilation of this information introduced delays and errors.
tldr.mechanism: Create a distributed database of network services where each server site maintains its own information locally, with a unified interface to access them—inspired by lessons from the Resources Notebook.
tldr.outcome: The proposal aims to put information responsibility closer to the source, reducing compilation overhead and errors, though implementation details are left to a future working group.

facts.label: Information location
facts.value: Local at each site, or at the NIC

today: This proposal predates modern web directories and search engines. The concept of distributed information maintained by sources and accessed by a unified mechanism became fundamental to how the internet works today.

sections.title: Growing Network, Growing Confusion
sections.content: The ARPANET was expanding to include users not tied to any server site. These new users needed information about which hosts offered what services and how to access them. Until then, the Resources Notebook had been the main source of network-wide information. However, maintaining a central notebook required many steps, delayed updates, and introduced errors as information passed through multiple people.
sections.eli5: The network was growing, and new users did not know what services were available or how to use them. The only guide was a notebook that got updated slowly.

sections.title: Distributed Information, Local Authority
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that each server site create and maintain its own information file, either locally or at the NIC (Network Information Center). Instead of a single source compiling everything, responsibility would be distributed: each site knows its own services best and should keep that information current.

The proposal also suggests defining a mechanism so users at different sites can access these distributed files using tools they already have.
sections.eli5: Instead of one person collecting information from everywhere, let each server site write down what it offers, and then provide one way for users to look it all up.

sections.title: Technical Considerations
sections.content:
One technical issue stands out: how to make these disparate files accessible to an automated tool. The NIC was working at the time to smooth the interface between NLS (a specialized editing system) and regular files. A distributed information system would benefit from this work, allowing both types of files to be queried in a uniform way.

The proposal is conceptual; the NIC suggested forming a working group to develop actual specifications.
sections.eli5: Different sites kept information in different formats. The hard part would be making one tool that can read them all.
